common_name: Cityline Berlin Hydrangea (Compact Pink-Blue Mophead Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Cityline Berlin holds rich pink tones in neutral-to-alkaline soil and shifts toward blue as soil acidity increases.

directions: Cityline Berlin is a compact bigleaf hydrangea in the city-named Cityline series, selected for a dense, rounded habit under 3 feet tall with sturdy stems that hold rounded mophead clusters of rich pink or blue upright without flopping. Glossy dark green foliage sets off the large flower heads, whose color follows the same aluminum-availability response typical of macrophylla hydrangeas — more blue in acidic soil, more pink as pH rises — and can be nudged bluer with soil sulfur or aluminum sulfate. Keep soil consistently moist and humus-rich in partial shade, since the large leaves wilt quickly in dry heat or strong sun. Prune only lightly to remove dead wood, since flowers form primarily on the previous season's growth and heavy pruning sacrifices the coming year's bloom.

common_name: Cityline Rio Hydrangea (Compact Electric Blue-Lavender Mophead Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Cityline Rio develops its most electric blue color in acidic soil and shifts toward vibrant lavender as soil pH rises.

directions: Cityline Rio is a compact bigleaf hydrangea in the Cityline series, holding a tidy, well-proportioned habit under 3 feet with strong stems that support its rounded mophead blooms without flopping. Flower color runs from electric blue in acidic soil to vibrant lavender as soil pH rises, following the standard aluminum-uptake color response of macrophylla hydrangeas, and can be pushed bluer with soil sulfur or aluminum sulfate. Its compact size suits foundation plantings, small beds, and large containers where full-sized hydrangeas would quickly outgrow the space. Keep soil consistently moist and humus-rich in partial shade, and prune only lightly to remove dead wood, since this cultivar blooms mainly on the previous season's growth.

common_name: Cityline Mars Hydrangea (Compact Picotee Mophead Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Cityline Mars develops indigo-blue centers in acidic soil and richer pink centers in alkaline soil, with white picotee edges on the florets persisting regardless of pH.

directions: Cityline Mars is a compact bigleaf hydrangea in the Cityline series, distinguished by rounded flower clusters whose florets show rich pink or indigo-blue centers edged in a thin band of white, a bicolor picotee effect that stands apart from the solid-colored mopheads typical of the genus. Like other macrophylla cultivars, the center color shifts with soil pH — bluer in acidic soil, pinker as pH rises — while the white edging stays constant; amend with soil sulfur or aluminum sulfate to intensify blue tones. Its dense, compact habit under 3 feet fits foundation plantings and containers. Keep soil consistently moist and humus-rich in partial shade, and prune only lightly to remove dead wood, since flowers form mainly on the previous season's growth.

common_name: Fasan Hydrangea (Teller Series Red-Pink Lacecap Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Fasan holds its strongest red-pink tones in neutral-to-alkaline soil, trending toward purple-red as soil acidity increases.

directions: Fasan is a lacecap member of the Teller series of bigleaf hydrangeas, introduced in the late 1970s and named for the German word for pheasant, a reference to the deep red-pink coloring reminiscent of the bird's wattle. It carries a flat outer ring of large, showy sterile florets in strong red-pink to purple-red tones surrounding a central disk of small fertile flowers, a more delicate and naturalistic look than the rounded mophead cultivars. Like other macrophylla cultivars its color shifts with soil pH, trending redder in neutral-to-alkaline soil and more purple in acidic soil; garden lime nudges it toward the strongest red. It blooms on old wood, so prune only right after flowering to shape, and give it partial shade with consistently moist, humus-rich soil to prevent wilting in summer heat.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Freudenstein's pink-to-mauve mophead flowers shift bluer in acidic soil and pinker as soil pH rises.

directions: Freudenstein is an older German mophead cultivar with an upright, bushy habit to around 4 feet and coarsely toothed dark green foliage. Rounded flower heads open pink to mauve in summer, shifting toward blue-purple in acidic soil and staying pinker in neutral-to-alkaline soil; amend with aluminum sulfate to intensify blue tones or garden lime to hold pink. It blooms on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering to shape, and give it morning sun with afternoon shade in hot climates. Keep soil consistently moist and humus-rich, since the large leaves wilt quickly in dry heat.

common_name: Hamburg Hydrangea (Classic Large Pink-Blue Mophead Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Hamburg's large mophead clusters open clear pink in alkaline soil and blue in acidic soil.

directions: Hamburg is a classic old German mophead cultivar, bred by Heinrich Schadendorf and introduced in 1931. It forms a large, vigorous shrub topped with big, rounded flower heads that open clear pink in alkaline soil or blue in acidic soil, following the standard aluminum-availability color response of macrophylla hydrangeas; amend with aluminum sulfate to intensify blue tones or garden lime to hold pink. It blooms on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering to shape, and give it morning sun with afternoon shade in hot climates to prevent wilting. Provide consistently moist, humus-rich soil, since the large plant and large leaves both demand steady moisture through summer heat.

common_name: Marechal Foch Hydrangea (Historic French Deep Blue-Pink Mophead Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Marechal Foch's tight, rounded flower heads open deep blue in acidic soil and pink in alkaline soil.

directions: Marechal Foch is a historic French mophead cultivar bred by Emile Mouillere and introduced in 1919, named for French army general Ferdinand Foch. It produces tight, rounded flower heads with entire-edged sepals in deep blue or pink depending on soil pH, and is notable for flowering on side shoots as well as main stems, which extends the bloom season longer than many older cultivars. Like other macrophylla cultivars its color shifts with soil pH — blue in acidic soil, pink in alkaline soil — and can be intensified with aluminum sulfate or garden lime respectively. It blooms primarily on old wood, so prune only right after flowering, and give it morning sun with afternoon shade in hot climates along with consistently moist, humus-rich soil.

common_name: Mariesii Lilacina Hydrangea (Historic Lemoine Lavender-Pink Lacecap Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Mariesii Lilacina's lacecap florets open lavender-blue in acidic soil and soft pink in alkaline soil.

directions: Mariesii Lilacina is one of the classic early-20th-century lacecap selections raised by the Lemoine nursery in France, closely related to 'Mariesii' and 'Mariesii Variegata' already grown for their flat, outer ring of large sterile florets surrounding a central disk of small fertile flowers. Its sterile ray florets open in soft lavender-pink tones that shift toward blue in acidic soil and toward clear pink as soil pH rises; amend with aluminum sulfate to intensify blue or garden lime to hold pink. It blooms on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering to shape, and give it morning sun with afternoon shade in hot climates. Provide consistently moist, humus-rich soil to prevent wilting during summer heat.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Tricolor's variegated foliage holds its cream-and-green pattern best in bright but filtered light, and reverts to solid green if deep shade or stray green-leaved shoots are left unpruned.

directions: Tricolor is a vigorous, tall-growing lacecap cultivar grown chiefly for its striking foliage, boldly variegated in deep green, light green, and creamy white. In late summer it produces loose, flat flower heads with soft cream sterile sepals surrounding small fertile flowers tinted blue or pink depending on soil pH. Because the variegation is somewhat unstable, prune out any branches that revert to solid green as soon as they appear to keep the plant's pattern strong. It blooms on old wood, so prune for shape only right after flowering, and give it partial shade with consistently moist, humus-rich soil — too much direct sun can scorch the pale foliage.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Quadricolor's yellow-and-cream leaf margins are brightest in filtered light and can revert to plain green on individual shoots, which should be pruned out.

directions: Quadricolor is a variegated lacecap cultivar closely related to and often confused with 'Tricolor', distinguished by leaf margins marked in yellow, cream, and both light and dark green rather than the cream-and-green pattern of Tricolor. It produces loose, flat flower heads in light blue or light pink depending on soil pH during late summer. Foliage color is notably unstable and prone to reverting to solid green, so prune out any all-green shoots promptly to preserve the variegated pattern. It blooms on old wood, so prune for shape only right after flowering, and provide partial shade with consistently moist, humus-rich soil to protect the pale leaf margins from scorching in strong sun.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Harlequin's floret centers shift between dark pink and bright blue depending on soil pH, while the thin white edge banding stays constant.

directions: Harlequin is grown for its unusual bicolor florets — pink to purple-blue centers edged in a thin band of white — a picotee pattern that rewards close viewing more than a mass display from a distance. As with other macrophylla cultivars, the colored portion of each floret shifts toward blue in acidic soil and toward dark pink in alkaline soil, while the white edging itself does not change; amend with aluminum sulfate or garden lime to push the center color further. The blooms are comparatively tender and should be shielded from afternoon sun, which fades the delicate bicolor pattern. It blooms on old wood, so prune only right after flowering, and keep soil consistently moist and humus-rich through summer heat.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Nigra's rounded flower heads open light rose-pink in alkaline soil and light blue in acidic soil.

directions: Nigra is distinguished from other mophead cultivars by its slender, near-black stems — the Latin name translates to 'black' — which provide ornamental interest year-round, even in winter after the leaves drop, much like the dark stems of 'Mathilda Gutges'. Large, rounded flower heads bloom from mid to late summer into fall in light rose-pink on alkaline soil or light blue on acidic soil, following the typical macrophylla color response; amend with aluminum sulfate to intensify blue tones. It blooms mainly on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering to shape, and give it partial shade with rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil to keep the large leaves from wilting in summer heat.
